The unexpected visitor
It was a quiet Sunday afternoon. Mary had just settled onto the sofa with a cup of tea when the doorbell rang.
On the doorstep stood a young man in a football jersey. “Good afternoon, Mrs. Johnson! Is Alex home?”
“No, dear. He’s out. Who are you?”
“Chris. One of his friends. We watched the match here last Saturday. Remember when Alex shouted after that missed penalty? I thought the neighbors were going to call the police!”
Mary laughed. “They nearly broke my ears!” She remembered the shouting, but not this young man.

“I’m actually a bit embarrassed,” Chris said. “I left my watch in Alex’s bedroom. My girlfriend gave it to me for my birthday. I took it off when we played video games upstairs. I think it’s on his desk.”
“Well, Alex isn’t here right now.”
“No problem. I’ll be thirty seconds. I tried calling, but he didn’t answer. I don’t want to bother him over something so silly.”
Mary looked toward the stairs. Alex did invite friends over, and she couldn’t possibly remember every face. Chris sounded familiar. His story was plausible. He was asking for a small favor.
Would you let him in?
A moment to decide
What would you do if you were Mary?
Choose a response to explore it. There is no score.
Let him enter
Mary still has not verified who Chris is. A friendly explanation can be persuasive, but the risk remains. His story might be true; she can check before granting access.
Call Alex first
Using the number she already trusts is a sensible independent check. Knowing who Chris is and confirming permission to enter are two separate questions.
Ask Chris to return when Alex is home
Mary can help without granting unverified access right now. Waiting is a reasonable option when she cannot verify the request.
A familiar detail is not proof

Before opening the door, Mary needs to ask a different question: what does she actually know? Chris knows Alex’s name, mentions a match that really happened, and behaves politely. None of those details proves that Alex knows him—or that Chris has permission to enter Alex’s bedroom.

He might be genuine. He might have picked up those details from a public post or overheard conversation. Mary does not have to accuse him of anything. She can simply call Alex on the number she already has, or ask Chris to return when Alex is home.
That pause is a useful starting point for understanding cybersecurity: someone can sound familiar without being verified.

Imagine your house opens with a secret code
Now replace Mary’s metal front-door key with a digital keypad. You type a secret phrase to unlock your home. Convenient: nothing to carry, and the code is stored in your memory.

But what if someone watches you type it? They may learn the code without ever touching your keys. And if you use the same code for your house, office, and storage room, discovering it could unlock all three.

That is how to think about passwords. A password is a secret used to authenticate you. A stolen or reused password can expose several accounts. Strong, unique passwords—ideally managed with a password manager—or passkeys make this much harder. A passkey is not simply another code to remember: it uses cryptographic credentials tied to the legitimate service and is resistant to many phishing attacks.
Some doors deserve another check
You might protect a garden shed with one lock but keep important documents inside a locked cabinet, too. The extra barrier matters if the first one fails.

Online, multifactor authentication (MFA) provides an additional sign-in check from a different factor, such as a security key or authenticator, alongside a password. It does not solve every threat, but it can help prevent a stolen password from being enough on its own.
The level of protection should fit the consequences: a public photo album and confidential financial records do not carry the same risk.
Trust does not mean every key

Imagine a trusted neighbor waters your plants while you travel. You may arrange access to the garden, but you would not also give them the combination to your safe or the keys to every private room. That is not an insult. Those permissions simply have nothing to do with watering plants.

The same logic applies at work. A receptionist might need appointment schedules, but not employee salary records. An accountant may need invoices, but not everyone’s email. People and applications should receive only the permissions required for their tasks, and only for as long as they are needed.

This is called the principle of least privilege. It reduces the harm that can result from mistakes, compromised accounts, or misuse. Even if Chris really is Alex’s friend, that friendship does not automatically authorize him to search Alex’s room.
And make sure the visitor has left

Permission also has an end. Suppose Mary verifies Chris’s identity, allows him to retrieve the watch, and then leaves for the shops without checking that he has gone. The visit might have started legitimately, but access should not remain open indefinitely.

Online, this is especially relevant on shared or public devices. Signing out of your accounts and closing authenticated sessions helps prevent the next user from entering as you. On your own devices, a strong screen lock, sensible session settings, and remote sign-out options add protection.
Beware the gift that opens another door

Another day, a visitor offers Mary a “free home-security upgrade.” He wears a shirt printed with a recognizable company logo and hands her a small device. “Just connect it to your home network,” he says. It looks official—but a logo on a shirt does not establish who he works for, and neat packaging does not establish what a device does.

This is a useful analogy for a Trojan: malicious software that pretends to be something legitimate or desirable. A fake app, attachment, or update may appear useful while doing something harmful after installation. Download from trustworthy sources, verify unexpected requests independently, and keep software updated. Even legitimate-looking downloads deserve attention to permissions and publisher identity.
So what is cybersecurity—and why should you care?

Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting devices, accounts, networks, information, and digital services from unauthorized access, manipulation, damage, and disruption. It includes technology, but also the decisions people make.

We protect confidentiality (who may see information), integrity (whether information remains correct), and availability (whether systems and files remain usable). The things at stake are ordinary: family photos, messages, bank accounts, schoolwork, customer details, and the ability for a small business to keep operating.

Good habits work together: pause at unexpected requests; verify through a number or website you find independently; use unique passwords or passkeys; enable MFA; give people and apps only necessary access; sign out of shared devices; update software; and back up files that matter.
Back at the doorstep, Mary smiles and says, “Let me call Alex first.” That is neither rude nor paranoid. It is a sensible check before opening a door.
Before you open the door to your digital world, make sure you know who is knocking—and what you are allowing inside.
